title: Comfort My People: The Incomparable God Comes
summary: The second major part of Isaiah opens with God's command to comfort Jerusalem: her hard service is over and her sin is pardoned. Voices call for a highway for the LORD through the wilderness, declare that all flesh is grass while God's word stands forever, and tell Zion to announce the good news that God is coming as a mighty king and a gentle shepherd. The rest of the chapter sets the Creator beside the nations, the idols, the rulers, and the stars, none of which compare to him, and ends with the promise that those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength.
story: Chapter 39 ended with a prediction that Judah's treasures and princes would be carried to Babylon. Chapter 40 speaks as though that has happened. The people addressed are worn out, their city has served its sentence, and some of them believe God has lost track of them (verse 27). Everything in chapters 40 to 55 grows from this opening: the return from exile pictured as a new exodus, God's argument against the idols of Babylon, the naming of Cyrus as the one who will release the captives, and the figure of the Servant of the LORD. The first half of Isaiah was mostly judgment with hope breaking through; now hope takes the lead, grounded in who God is.
historical:
Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC. The temple was burned, the monarchy ended, and many of Judah's leading families were deported to Babylonia, where they lived for decades. In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus captured Babylon, and in 539/538 BC he allowed exiled peoples, including the Judeans, to return home and rebuild their sanctuaries. Chapters 40 to 55 speak into the last years of the exile, looking toward that release.

How the book came to address that situation is one of the classic questions of Old Testament study, and it arises here because the setting changes so sharply. The traditional view, held by Jewish and Christian readers for most of history and defended today by scholars such as J. Alec Motyer and John Oswalt, is that Isaiah of Jerusalem, in the eighth century BC, was given these words for a generation not yet born, and that the book's own claim to foretell events (41:21-29; 44:24-28) is part of its message. Most critical scholars since the late eighteenth century assign chapters 40 to 55 to an anonymous prophet of the exile, often called Second Isaiah, because these chapters assume the fall of Jerusalem as past and speak of Cyrus as a figure already on the scene. Many in both camps now read the book as a deliberately unified whole, noting that its themes, such as the Holy One of Israel, run through both halves. The introduction to Isaiah sets out these positions more fully.
cultural:
In Babylon, the great religious festivals included processions in which the images of the gods were carried along broad ceremonial roads. The exiles would have known that world well. Isaiah 40 imagines a different road: not built by kings for idols to be carried, but a highway in the wilderness on which the living God himself comes to his people, with valleys raised and mountains lowered. Ancient kings also sent heralds ahead of them to announce their arrival and to see that roads were made ready, and the chapter uses that royal picture.

The description of idol-making in verses 19 and 20 reflects how cult statues were actually produced: a craftsman cast a figure, a goldsmith covered it, and it was fixed in place so that it would not fall over. A poor worshiper chose a durable wood. The picture of the shepherd in verse 11 drew on the ancient habit of calling kings shepherds of their people. Here the King who comes with a strong arm also carries lambs close to his heart and leads the nursing ewes gently, as a real shepherd had to.
literary: The chapter is poetry built from voices. Verses 1 to 11 form a prologue in which unnamed speakers, perhaps members of God's heavenly council, take up God's command to comfort: one voice calls for a highway (verses 3 to 5), another commissions a herald who asks what to cry (verses 6 to 8), and Zion is sent up a mountain to announce God's arrival (verses 9 to 11). Verses 12 to 31 shift to disputation, a form of argument with rhetorical questions: Who has measured the waters? To whom will you liken God? Do you not know? Have you not heard? The questions pile up to overturn the people's complaint that God has forgotten them. The two halves are linked by the contrast between human weakness (grass, grasshoppers, stubble, weary youths) and the strength of God, which he gives to the faint.

outline.t: Comfort for Jerusalem: the sentence served, the sin pardoned
A highway for the LORD in the wilderness
All flesh is grass, but God's word stands forever
Good news for Zion: God comes as king and shepherd
The Creator beside rulers and stars
Strength for the weary who wait on the LORD

doctrines.note: The chapter is one of Scripture's great statements of God's incomparability. He measures the waters in his hand, needs no counselor, calls the stars by name, and “will not grow tired or weary.” Nothing in creation, whether nation, ruler, or idol, can be set beside him.

“The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.” Everything human fades, but what God has spoken holds. The promises of the coming chapters are to be trusted because of whose word they are.
Comfort begins with pardon: Jerusalem's “iniquity has been pardoned.” God's return to his people rests on his dealing with their sin, a theme that deepens until chapter 53.
Waiting on the LORD is not passive resignation but confident expectation, and the chapter ties it to renewed strength. The weary people are given not a plan but a vision of God.

words.note: Nacham, to comfort. The repeated command that opens the chapter sets the tone for all that follows. The comfort is not merely soothing words; it is the announcement that the sentence is over and that God is coming to act.

Basar, to bring good news. Zion and Jerusalem are called heralds of good news in verse 9. The Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) rendered this verb with the word from which the New Testament's word for “gospel” comes, and the early Christians heard in these chapters the language of the good news about Jesus.

Chesed, usually loyal love or steadfast kindness, here rendered “glory” in verse 6. Human chesed, even at its best, is like a flower of the field: it does not last. The contrast is with God's word, which stands forever. Elsewhere the same word describes God's own covenant faithfulness, which is exactly what humans cannot match.

Qavah, to wait for or hope in, with a sense of tense, expectant looking. “Those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength.” The word joins waiting to trust: those who wait are staking their future on God's coming.

christ: The New Testament uses this chapter at the very start of the gospel story. All four Gospels identify John the Baptist as the voice calling in the wilderness to prepare the way for the Lord (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4-6; John 1:23). The implication is striking: the LORD whose way John prepares is Jesus, and the God who comes to his people in Isaiah 40 comes in him. The Jewish community at Qumran also applied verse 3 to itself, going out into the desert to prepare the way, which shows how alive this text was in expectation before Jesus. First Peter 1:24-25 quotes the passage about grass and flowers and identifies the enduring word of God with the good news preached to its readers. Paul draws on verse 13 (“Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD?”) in Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16. And the shepherd who carries the lambs finds its echo in Jesus's description of himself as the good shepherd in John 10.

hard.q: If chapters 40 to 55 address the exiles in Babylon, did Isaiah of Jerusalem write them a century and a half in advance, or did a later prophet?
hard.a:
Both positions are held by serious readers who take the text seriously. The case for a later prophet rests on the setting: these chapters do not predict the fall of Jerusalem so much as assume it, speak comfort to people already in exile, and name Cyrus as God's agent in a way that suggests he is already active. On this view the book was expanded by a prophet standing in Isaiah's tradition, and the whole was gathered under his name. The case for Isaiah's authorship rests on the book's own presentation of itself as one prophecy, the New Testament's citation of both halves as Isaiah (for example John 12:38-41), continuity of vocabulary and themes across the book, and, most of all, the claim these chapters make that the LORD alone can announce things before they happen. Defenders argue that ruling out prediction in advance would silence the chapters' central argument.

A third group reads the book as a unity shaped over time, holding that its canonical form is the one the church received and should interpret. Whatever one concludes, the chapters speak to people in exile, and they are best understood by reading them from that place: worn out, in a foreign land, wondering whether God still sees.

questions: The people complained, “My way is hidden from the LORD.” When have you felt that God had lost track of you, and how does this chapter answer that feeling?
The chapter pictures God as both a mighty king and a gentle shepherd. Which of these do you find easier to believe, and why?
All flesh is grass, but God's word stands forever. What in your life are you treating as permanent that is actually grass?
